# The Art of Not Knowing Where You're Going

There is something quietly radical about a walk without a destination. Not a jog with a fitness tracker counting every step, not a march toward a known address, but a genuine amble — the kind where you turn left simply because the light looked interesting on that particular street. We've somehow convinced ourselves that movement without purpose is wasted movement. I think it might be the most purposeful thing a person can do.

I keep thinking about how much of modern life is engineered to eliminate wandering. Every app wants a destination. Every search engine demands a query. Every playlist is algorithmically generated to keep you engaged, to predict what you'll want next before you've finished wanting what you have now. Even the language of self-improvement is saturated with targets and KPIs and optimization. We optimize our mornings, our sleep cycles, our protein intake. We track our screen time while feeling anxious about our screen time, which only increases our screen time. It's a strange loop, and most of us are caught in it without quite realizing the shape of the trap.

But the mind — the real mind, the one underneath the productivity apps and the morning routines — that mind is a wandering thing. It's built for drifting. Think about the last truly great idea you had. I would bet it didn't arrive while you were staring at a blank document trying to have a great idea. It arrived in the shower, or on a long drive, or at 2 a.m. when you were supposed to be sleeping. It arrived because you were wandering.

Neuroscience has a name for this: the default mode network. It's the part of your brain that lights up when you're not focused on anything in particular — when your mind is free to drift, to make unexpected connections, to rehearse possible futures and reconsider the past. For years, researchers thought this was just the brain idling. We now understand it's the brain doing some of its deepest work. Daydreaming isn't the absence of thinking. It's thinking without a leash.

I wonder if we've built an entire civilization on the premise that the leash is better.

Consider the conversations we have. When was the last time you had a conversation that genuinely meandered — one that started with someone's grocery list and ended up somewhere around the meaning of loss, or a strange coincidence, or an old movie you both half-remember? Those conversations are becoming rare. We text in bursts. We communicate in reaction emojis. We've started to think of conversation as a series of information transfers rather than an act of mutual exploration. But the best conversations aren't informational. They're generative. You don't exchange ideas in them — you build ideas together, slowly, hesitantly, without knowing where the thought will end up. That's wandering with another person, and it is one of the great joys of being alive.

There's a book I think about often — Rebecca Solnit's *Wanderlust: A History of Walking*. She writes about how walking has been both a tool of empire and a tool of revolution. Soldiers and generals walked to conquer, but philosophers and poets walked to think. Rousseau insisted he could only compose while walking. Wordsworth reportedly walked 250,000 miles in his lifetime. Thoreau wrote, "I think that I cannot preserve my health and spirits, unless I spend four hours a day at least — and it is commonly more than that — sauntering through the woods and over the hills and fields, absolutely free from all worldly engagements." Four hours a day. Imagine that. Imagine what kind of civilization we would build if we thought four hours of sauntering was non-negotiable.

I think about children, too. Watch a child in a yard sometime. They don't move from Point A to Point B. They find a stick and the stick becomes a sword, then a fishing rod, then a divining rod for underground rivers. They kneel in the dirt for twenty minutes watching an ant carry something impossibly heavy. They don't experience this as a waste of time. They experience it as the entirety of time. That's not childish. That might be the most sophisticated relationship with existence any of us ever achieve.

Somewhere along the way, we trade that for efficiency. We learn to walk with purpose. We learn that a detour is a delay. We learn that wondering without concluding is inefficient, that curiosity without application is indulgent, that rest without recovery is laziness. And so we fill every silence and every pause and every gap in our schedules until we are running — not toward anything, exactly, but away from the terrifying possibility of doing nothing.

But doing nothing is not doing nothing. It's where you meet yourself. It's where memory and imagination sit down at the same table and start talking to each other. It's where you discover that you have questions you didn't know you had, desires you've been too busy to hear, griefs that have been waiting patiently for a quiet moment to surface.

I don't want to romanticize this beyond all reason. The world has real urgencies. Bills need paying, systems need fixing, injustices need confronting. I'm not arguing for an entirely unmoored life. But I am arguing that the space between the urgencies — the unplanned hour, the conversation that goes nowhere useful, the walk that doesn't count toward anything — that space is not empty. It is full. It is full of everything we say we care about but somehow never schedule time for: wonder, reflection, creativity, connection, peace.

So here is my small, unscientific prescription. Sometime this week, go somewhere without deciding where. Talk to someone without having an agenda. Sit still and let your mind do whatever it wants for ten minutes. You'll feel unproductive. You'll feel the itch of that voice that says you should be doing something. Let it itch. Then watch what rises in the quiet underneath it.

You might not find an answer to anything. But you might find better questions. And better questions, in my experience, are worth a great deal more.
